raw_case_text:
In July 2022, a 56-year-old Chinese male came to our hospital for 20 days of diarrhea. At the beginning, it is yellow loose stools, 6-8 times a day. Ten days ago, the patient had aggravated diarrhea, manifested as dark green watery stool, up to 10 times a day, accompanied by palpitations, shortness of breath, dizziness, dry mouth, dry skin, and sunken eye socket symptoms. A week before his admission, he had no history of fevering, abdominal pain or travelling. Two years ago, the patient received allograft in our hospital for liver cancer and hepatitis B cirrhosis. To avoid rejection, he took long-term immunosuppressive therapy of tacrolimus (1mg q12h), mycophenolic acid (750mg q12h) and sirolimus (1mg qd) after surgery.
On admission, the patient had a temperature of 37.9  C, presented with septic shock and metabolic acidosis, and was intubated and transferred to the intensive care unit. Because the patient presented with oliguria and serum creatinine of 170 mumol/L, continuous renal replacement treatment (CRRT) was conducted for acute kidney injury. In addition, laboratory examination revealed white blood cell (WBC) count 13.46x109/L with an elevated neutrophil ratio of 87.9%. The concentration of procalcitonin (PCT) and C-reactive protein (CRP) were 3.32 ng/mL and 190 mg/L, respectively. Troponin-T (TPN-T) was 191.2 ng/L. It suggested possible abdominal or lung infection and myocardial injury. There were no significant changes in liver function test, blood coagulation test or platelet count. The tacrolimus concentration is within the target treatment range. As the patient's temperature continued to rise to 38.5 C, no significant improvement was observed after empirical treatment with piperacillin/tazobactam, we collected bronchoalveolar lavage solution for culture. The results revealed Aspergillus fumigatus and carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae. Urine bacterial culture, venous blood culture and anaerobic blood culture were negative. According to drug sensitivity results, antibacterial agents were replaced by meropenem and voriconazole. In view of the severe infection of patients and the fact that the concentrations of tacrolimus and sirolimus can be affected by voriconazole, tacrolimus and sirolimus were discontinued. We collected stool for detection, and the results showed that intestinal bacterial culture, microscopic examination of parasite, clostridium difficile antigen were negative. Because of diarrhea, the patient was given compound berberine (a Chinese proprietary medicine, which has inhibitory effect on intestinal bacteria and can be used for intestinal infection) to decrease diarrhea, and at the same time, the electrolyte balance and acid-base balance in the patient's body were corrected. Subsequently, the patient's diarrhea was significantly mitigated, and enteral nutrition solution and probiotics were given to regulate intestinal function. Two days later, the patient again developed high frequency diarrhea (6-8 watery stools per day) with fever, with a temperature fluctuating around 39  C. Subsequently, parasitic examination of stool and fecal bacterial cultures received negative results. For rapid detection of possible pathogens, the blood sample of the patient was sent to undergo PACEseq mNGS analysis (Genskey, Chengdu, China). Two days later, the mNGS result revealed the presence of Klebsiella pneumoniae and Cryptosporidium parvum, with reads of 19 and 33, respectively (Figure 1). In addition, we detected oval bodies in stool samples of patients by modified acid-fast stain, which were Cryptosporidium oocysts. At present, Cryptosporidium infection was well established, and we proposed to give nitazoxanide, but this drug is not readily available. Therefore, we temporarily chose azithromycin (0.5g qd) alone for treatment. At the same time, laboratory results indicated that the indices of the liver function and T lymphocyte count were elevated, which may be related to the rejection caused by the reduction of immunosuppressive drugs. Hence we added cyclosporine (150mg bid) into his prescription. Two days after taking cyclosporine, we determined that the trough concentration of cyclosporine was 194.00 mug/L, which exceeded the therapeutic concentration, possibly related to the combination of Voriconazole, and adjusted the cyclosporine dose to maintain around 100 ng/mL. After one week, the patient's diarrhea did not improve, so azithromycin was stopped and nitazoxanide (500mg tid) was added. On the third day of medication, the patient's diarrhea frequency was reduced to 3-4 times a day. After two weeks of treatment, the patient's diarrhea subsided. The fecal samples were collected again for acid fast staining, and we found no Cryptosporidium oocysts and stopped providing nitazoxanide. 
The patient recovered slowly with immunosuppression and severe pulmonary infection. After 40 days of hospitalization, the patient's systemic infection was obviously controlled, and he could be disconnected from the ventilator intermittently. At the same time, the creatinine slowly decreased to the normal baseline level, and the liver function gradually recovered. After 47 days in hospital, the patient's condition gradually stabilized. He no longer relied on the ventilator and was transferred to the general ward to continue rehabilitation treatment. The timeline of the treatment is shown in Figure 2.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 56-year-old male liver transplant recipient presented with a 20-day history of worsening watery diarrhea accompanied by palpitations, shortness of breath, and dizziness.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: In July 2022, the patient developed yellow loose stools (6-8 times/day) that worsened 10 days prior to admission to dark green watery stools (up to 10 times/day), accompanied by palpitations, dyspnea, dizziness, dry mouth, dry skin, and sunken eyes, culminating in septic shock, metabolic acidosis, and oliguria on admission.
subjective.past_medical_history: Orthotopic liver transplantation 2 years prior for hepatocellular carcinoma and hepatitis B cirrhosis; maintained on long-term tacrolimus (1 mg q12h), mycophenolic acid (750 mg q12h), and sirolimus (1 mg daily).
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for severe watery diarrhea, palpitations, shortness of breath, dizziness, dry mouth, dry skin, sunken eyes, and oliguria; negative for pre-admission fever, abdominal pain, or recent travel.

objective.physical_examination: Admitted with temperature 37.9 C (later spiking to 38.5-39 C), signs of severe dehydration (dry mouth, dry skin, sunken eye sockets), and septic shock requiring endotracheal intubation and ICU admission.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs showed metabolic acidosis, acute kidney injury with serum creatinine 170 umol/L, leukocytosis (WBC 13.46 x 10^9/L, 87.9% neutrophils), procalcitonin 3.32 ng/mL, CRP 190 mg/L, and troponin-T 191.2 ng/L; baseline liver function tests, coagulation profile, platelet count, and tacrolimus trough level were within normal/target ranges. Blood and urine bacterial cultures, routine stool bacterial cultures, routine stool microscopy, and stool Clostridioides difficile antigen were negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) culture grew Aspergillus fumigatus and carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae (CRKP). Blood PACEseq mNGS detected Cryptosporidium parvum (33 reads) and Klebsiella pneumoniae (19 reads), and modified acid-fast staining of stool confirmed oval Cryptosporidium oocysts.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Cryptosporidium parvum enteritis complicated by septic shock, acute kidney injury, and severe pulmonary co-infection with Aspergillus fumigatus and carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae (CRKP) in an immunosuppressed liver transplant recipient, confirmed by blood mNGS, modified acid-fast stool staining for Cryptosporidium oocysts, and BALF fungal/bacterial cultures. Treated with mechanical ventilation, CRRT, meropenem, and voriconazole (with discontinuation of tacrolimus/sirolimus and TDM-guided switch to cyclosporine to prevent rejection and drug interactions), plus nitazoxanide 500 mg three times daily for 2 weeks (after initial compound berberine and azithromycin failed). Diarrhea resolved with negative repeat stool acid-fast staining, renal and hepatic function normalized, and the patient was successfully weaned off mechanical ventilation and transferred to the general ward on hospital day 47.
